Stated Claim / Post Context:
How DBT treats borderline personality disorder, eating disorders and more | CNN

Developed by Dr. Marsha Linehan, DBT has helped many mental health patients build ‘a life worth living.’

Actual Article Body:
Dr. Marsha M. Linehan, creator of the lifesaving, gold standard treatment for borderline personality disorder and more, died Tuesday at 83, professionals who worked with her confirmed with CNN.

Linehan developed dialectical behavior therapy, or DBT, in the 1980s, basing its emotion regulation and distress-tolerance skills partly on cognitive behavioral therapy and elements of Zen Buddhism — including mindfulness and the dynamic balance of acceptance and change.

In addition to being highly suicidal, patients Linehan treated with DBT also typically had a complex array of issues that can be difficult to treat, including other psychological and behavioral problems, substance use disorders, eating disorders and more.

Principal among those is BPD, “a notoriously challenging condition to deal with,” Linehan wrote in her 2020 memoir “Building a Life Worth Living.”

Dialectical behavior therapy greatly differed from other therapies of the 1970s and 1980s and was heavily influenced by Linehan’s spiritual journey to becoming a Zen master. Her incorporation of mindfulness into psychotherapy was a first for Western psychiatry.

“I had to battle to have my radical ideas and approach to therapy accepted by my peers and by the world of psychiatry,” Linehan wrote.

Linehan revealed in 2011 that her work was motivated by her firsthand experience with BPD, which she had begun struggling with in high school. Then, she was one of the popular girls, often organizing concert outings or snack runs for her peers, Linehan wrote. But her transformation from her junior to senior year was stark — going from Mardi Gras queen nominee to resident in a double-secured unit at a psychiatric hospital.

Linehan’s confident, spirited sense of self had waned over that period. She had been feeling terribly inadequate and losing her ability to regulate her intense emotions and behaviors.

Living at a psychiatric hospital in 1961, Linehan, then 18, “was drowning in an ocean of self-loathing and shame, of feeling unloved and unlovable, and of indescribable emotional agony, so much so that I wanted to be dead,” she wrote. Linehan’s admission into the hospital for initially two weeks of diagnostic evaluation was per the recommendation of her psychiatrist, whose expertise Linehan’s parents sought since she had also been experiencing debilitating headaches and social withdrawal.
